hints: The output has one value for every depth of the tree.
Process all nodes that are currently at the same depth before moving to their children.
Keep a maximum value for the current level, then enqueue the next level.
Remember that node values can be as small as -2^31, so initialize the level maximum safely.
title: Determine Largest Value in Each Tree Row

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree will be in the range [0, 10^4].
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: At depth 0 the maximum is 1, at depth 1 the maximum is 3, and at depth 2 the maximum is 9.
The root contributes 1 at depth 0; the two children contribute a maximum of 3 at depth 1.

content.problemStatement:
With the `root` of a binary tree, output *an array of the largest value in each row* of the tree **(0-indexed)**.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2020/08/21/largest_e1.jpg)

```
Input: root = [1,3,2,5,3,null,9]
Output: [1,3,9]
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: root = [1,2,3]
Output: [1,3]
```

**Constraints:**

* The number of nodes in the tree will be in the range `[0, 10^4]`.
* `-2^31 <= Node.val <= 2^31 - 1`

notes: The level boundary is captured before processing each row, so values from different depths are never mixed.
The minimum int32 value is a valid node value, so the per-level maximum must be initialized to INT_MIN or its language equivalent.
An iterative traversal avoids recursion-depth issues on highly skewed trees with up to 10^4 nodes.
solution.approach: Traverse the tree level by level with breadth-first search. For each level, inspect all nodes currently in the queue, track the maximum value, and then enqueue their children for the next level. An empty tree returns an empty array.

better.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion-stack space, in addition to the result array.
better.description: Use depth-first search while carrying the current depth. On the first visit to a depth, store the node value; on later visits, update that depth's maximum. This visits each node once.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(w) auxiliary queue space, where w is the maximum tree width.
optimal.description: Use breadth-first search and process the queue one level at a time. The queue size at the start of a level gives the exact number of nodes in that row; compute its maximum while enqueuing the next row.

bruteForce.complexity: O(nh) worst-case time and O(h) traversal-stack space, where h is the tree height.
bruteForce.description: For every depth, perform a separate traversal from the root that visits only nodes at that depth and computes the maximum. Repeating these traversals can revisit the same nodes many times.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the tree, because every node is visited exactly once.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(w) auxiliary space for the BFS queue, where w is the maximum number of nodes at any one level; w is O(n) in the worst case.

followUps: Can you solve the problem with DFS instead of BFS while keeping O(n) time?
How would the auxiliary space change between BFS and DFS on a very wide tree versus a highly skewed tree?
How would you adapt the traversal if the tree were streamed level by level rather than stored in memory?

learningObjectives: Traverse a binary tree by levels using BFS.
Maintain an aggregate value independently for each tree depth.
Handle empty, sparse, skewed, balanced, duplicate-heavy, negative, and integer-boundary trees.
Analyze the relationship between tree height, width, time complexity, and auxiliary space.
